items.q: Fixing typos, removing duplicates and dropping impossible values is…
A value far outside the rest, like "200 lunches" on a normal day, is an…
A survey row says a student has "twelvety" pets. What should you do?
choices: keep it, every row is data
change every row to match it
fix or remove the row before charting
items.why: 'Twelvety' is not a number, so the row would poison the chart. Fix it or take it out first.

items.q: "Blue", "blue" and "Blu" appear in one column. Before charting you should…
items.why: The three spellings mean one color. Merging them makes one honest count instead of three small ones.

items.q: Comparing 12 of 20 in one class and 15 of 30 in another fairly needs…
items.why: The classes are different sizes, so raw counts mislead. Percentages put both on the same scale.

items.q: A rule or simulation that predicts what will happen is a…
Your paper ramp rule predicted 40 cm; five trials averaged 52 cm. What next?
choices: keep the rule as it is
change the rule and test again
items.why: The trials beat the rule by a lot, so the rule is wrong somewhere. Change it, then test the new rule.

items.q: After a change, the model's error went from 12 to 3. What does that show?
choices: the refined model fits the data better
the data from the trials is wrong
the trials were too short to count
items.why: Error measures the gap between the model and the data. A smaller error means the model fits better.

items.q: Your runner's jump rule: only 4 of 20 test runs finished; the target is about 16. You should…
choices: ship it, a hard game is a good game
change the jump rule and run the 20 tests again
run 2 more tests and call it done
remove the jump from the game
items.why: The rule fails most runs, far from the target. Change the rule and rerun the full set of tests.

items.q: Getting ideas or answers from many people, like a class survey, is…

choices: "Don't you agree recess is too short?"
items.why: The question pushes toward one answer ('Don't you agree'), so it leads people instead of asking fairly.

items.q: Why pool every pair's results on the projector?
choices: many contributors make a bigger, fairer sample
one pair's data is always enough
items.why: More answers from more people make the sample bigger and fairer, so the claim stands on more ground.

items.q: 28 of 30 students answered. The two missing answers…
choices: are an error in the app
items.why: Two answers can flip a close result, so missing answers matter most when the counts are near.
